To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in AMD, monocular fixation stability is poor and improves with time.
in patients with age related macular degeneration, monocular fixations with the worse eye are unstable and improve with time.
fixation stability did not change during binocular viewing in both groups, both conditions for controls and with the better eye in AMD patients.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stability of fixation in patients with AMD is poor and improves with time during monocular viewing, but not during binocular viewing.

fixation stability is stable over time in patients with AMD during both binocular and monocalar viewing, except for a linear improvement with time in fixation stability during monocular viewing of the worse eye in patients with AMD.
fixation stability is not affected in AMD patients during binocular viewing and is not affected in control participants or AMD patients during monocular viewing of the better eye.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
patients with AMD have difficulty maintaining fixation with the worse eye and this difficulty improves with time.
fixation stability is a dynamic process and that it is not static, as previously thought.
the worse eye in AMD has poor fixational control that can improve over a short time period.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fixation instability is a dynamic process that changes over time.
patients with maculopathy may be able to use the better eye to stabilize the gaze during reading, but this is not always possible.
patients with AMD may be able to improve fixation stability with practice, and this could potentially be exploited in a clinical setting to improve reading performance in patients with maculopathy.
